name: Q-switched / picosecond laser for dark circles
lead: Q-switched and picosecond lasers are short-pulse lasers that dermatologists use on tattoos and pigmentation. In appearance communities they are discussed as a way to lighten periorbital hyperpigmentation, the brown-pigment type of dark circle, so the skin under the eyes looks more even in tone and the face looks more rested.[1][2][3]

Q-switching builds up energy inside the laser and then releases it as a single, very short, intense pulse.[1] Q-switched lasers, with Nd:YAG types commonly favoured, are used for tattoo removal and for dark spots and other pigmentation problems.[1] Wikipedia dates the picosecond tattoo laser to 2013.[1] The pulses are meant to break pigment into particles that the body then clears.[1][11]

Dark circles have many causes, including thin skin showing blood vessels, hollowing, allergies and rubbing, and extra melanin around the eyes. The pigment type is the natural target for pigment lasers.[2][3] Dermatology literature discusses Q-switched Nd:YAG lasers for conditions such as melasma, lentigines and freckles, and a French review notes lasers are very effective for many hyperpigmented lesions but not for all kinds of pigmentation.[4][5]

chain: Pigment is fragmented and cleared over sessions
Under-eye skin tone looks lighter and more even
angle.text: People with brown, pigment-type dark circles look at pigment lasers to even out the skin under the eyes. The treatment is done in a dermatology clinic over a series of sessions.

infobox: Tattoo work typically takes many sessions at least a month apart[1]
Tattoo removal usually takes multiple sessions eight or more weeks apart [11]

paras: In active Q-switching an external switch controls release of stored laser energy; in passive Q-switching a saturable absorber does so. Compared with mode locking, Q-switching yields lower repetition rates and higher pulse energy.[1] In tattoo treatment, the pulses fragment ink particles that the lymphatic system clears, and full removal typically takes many sessions.[1]

Periorbital hyperpigmentation is described as an inherited trait of extra melanin, most prevalent at ages 16 to 25.[2] Wikipedia's overview of dark circles lists thin skin, bony structure, allergies, sun exposure, ageing and other contributors alongside pigment, and names lasers and intense pulsed light among specialist treatments.[3]

Wikipedia's tattoo removal article says short-pulsed laser effects on tattoos were first reported in the late 1960s, that Q-switched lasers became commercially practical in the late 1980s, and that the theory behind laser removal is selective photothermolysis, described by Anderson and Parrish in 1983.[11] Picosecond lasers followed, with the Q-switching article dating the picosecond tattoo laser to 2013 and the tattoo removal article describing anecdotal claims that picosecond alexandrite lasers clear ink faster.[1][11] The step from tattoos to pigment problems such as lentigines, freckles and Ota nevus has been described in dermatology reviews of laser therapy.[4]

Wikipedia's dark circles article lists pigment (excess melanin, sun exposure), vascular causes (dilated vessels showing through thin skin), structural causes (bone structure, orbicularis oculi prominence, fat loss and hollowing with age) and other contributors such as eye rubbing, allergies and fatigue.[3] The same article names laser and intense pulsed light treatment, low-level laser therapy, fat transplantation and hyaluronic acid fillers among options without reporting how well they work.[3] Pigment lasers are aimed at the melanin type; people whose circles come from hollowing or visible vessels are described as having different treatment routes, such as filler.[3]

Wikipedia describes the mechanism for tattoo ink: it absorbs the laser energy in nanoseconds, heats rapidly and shatters, and macrophages carry the fragments away, with fading gradual over the healing period.[11] In that setting about half of patients have temporary pigment changes that usually resolve within 6 to 12 months, hyperpigmentation is more common in skin types IV to VI and hypopigmentation more common in darker skin with higher energy and more frequent sessions, and scarring and blistering are rare.[11]

Wikipedia's dark circles article lists laser and intense pulsed light treatment among the options, alongside low-level laser therapy, autologous fat transplantation and hyaluronic acid fillers, and says dark circles tend to become more noticeable and more permanent with age.[3] Among topicals it names vitamin C, which it says may help brighten pigment and thicken the dermal layer so the circles are less visible, citing a 2009 study of lower-eyelid dark circles, and caffeine, described as a vasoconstrictor that tightens dilated vessels under the eye.[3]

It also notes that hydroquinone, once mixed into lightening moisturisers, has been banned for skin whitening in European countries and that the US FDA revoked its approval for over-the-counter hydroquinone preparations in 2006.[3] The article is flagged as needing more citations, and it gives no efficacy figures for the laser options.[3]

People who discuss under-eye darkness as a hardmaxxing topic list pigment lasers alongside peels, topical brighteners and microneedling as clinic options for the pigment type of dark circle. Hydroquinone, once common in lightening creams, has been restricted in Europe and lost over-the-counter approval in the US in 2006, according to Wikipedia.[3]

No studies found that test Q-switched or picosecond lasers specifically for under-eye dark circles in a reliable trial. A 2024 randomized trial that compared stromal vascular fraction, platelet-rich plasma and a 1064-nm Q-switched Nd:YAG laser for infraorbital dark circles has been retracted.[6]

Related research covers other pigmentation. A French review reports that lasers are a standard treatment for actinic lentigos and dermal hypermelanocytosis such as Ota nevus, that freckles and cafe-au-lait macules relapse almost constantly, and that Q-switched lasers at standard parameters are not recommended for melasma because of relapses and post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation.[4] A 2009 trial of 45 Egyptian patients compared hydroquinone, trichloroacetic acid peels and frequency-doubled Q-switched Nd:YAG laser for melasma.[7] A 2024 randomized trial compared home-based 590 nm LED with in-hospital 1064 nm Q-switched Nd:YAG for facial melasma,[8] and a 2025 trial studied Q-switched Nd:YAG combined with medical therapy for hyperpigmentation.[9] A 2023 split-lesion trial compared picosecond and Q-switched 532 nm Nd:YAG lasers for ephelides (freckles).[10]

Dermatology reviews associate Q-switched lasers on melasma with relapse and post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation.[4] The skin around the eyes is thin and close to the eye, which is why laser work in the area is performed by trained clinicians.[3]

timeline.event: Anderson and Parrish describe selective photothermolysis.[11]
Q-switched lasers become commercially practical for tattoo removal.[11]
Picosecond tattoo laser introduced, per Wikipedia.[1]
Randomized trial compares picosecond and Q-switched 532 nm lasers for freckles.[10]

card.summary: Short-pulse pigment lasers used on periorbital darkness; a real dermatology tool for pigment, with little published under-eye evidence found here.
card.aka: Q-switched Nd:YAG, picosecond laser, laser toning
card.note: Pigment lasers are clinic procedures; side effects are not well covered.

quick.overview:
Q-switched and picosecond lasers deliver extremely short, intense pulses of light. In dermatology they are used on tattoos and on dark spots and other pigmentation problems, and some people apply the idea to periorbital hyperpigmentation, the pigment-type dark circle.
No trials of these lasers for dark circles have been published, so evidence for that use is limited.
quick.mechanism: Q-switching stores energy in the laser and releases it as one giant short pulse. In tattoo work the pulses shatter ink into particles the body clears; the same pulse physics is applied to pigment. A picosecond laser was introduced in 2013 for hard-to-remove inks.
quick.risks: Periorbital skin is thin and close to the eye, so laser procedures there are done by clinicians; no regulatory details specific to this use are given here.
